papers.title: Enhanced image forensics through partial C2PA-based provenance information
papers.abstract: Cryptographically verifiable C2PA-based Content Credentials (CCs) can be attached to freshly acquired or generated digital images but also to already existing ones with no previous provenance information, for instance after processing through trusted C2PA-enabled software tools. The latter case leads to images with so-called partial CCs, which capture only the last operations applied, while prior provenance remains unknown and can be investigated through signal forensics. This paper addresses the forensic analysis of such images, highlighting the opportunity to leverage the partial CCs as additional trusted knowledge to adapt forensic detectors towards the statistical characteristics of the image under analysis and mitigate potential distribution shifts. To this end, a two-step strategy is envisioned: (i) reconstructing the operations applied by the last signer through a structural analysis of the partial CCs; (ii) exploiting the obtained reconstruction to enhance the forensic detector of the analyst through an adaptation process. An empirical analysis on partial CCs produced by commercial C2PA-enabled software tools through different editing operations is carried out, providing evidence on the feasibility of the reconstruction in practical cases. An experimental case study on the forensic task of synthetic image detection is then presented, showing that the proposed strategy can significantly enhance the performance of state-of-the-art detectors on test images that are postprocessed via C2PA-enabled software tools after being generated/acquired.

papers.title: Cassette-Editor: A Video Editing Agent That Edits the Way You Do
papers.abstract: Language agents increasingly work by calling tools on a persistent artifact, such as a code repository, and the result of each call shapes their next step. Video editing is a demanding case of this pattern: what a frame shows depends on how every clip is trimmed, retimed, cropped, and nested, so knowledge about the footage holds only for particular uses of it, and an invalid edit can leave the timeline structurally broken. Existing video editing agents keep their edits valid with critic agents, reviewers, or restricted output formats. We present Cassette-Editor, a video editing agent with a deliberately simple interface: one tool reads the project and one tool writes to it. Every write passes through the same executor, rules, and commit service as the user's manual edits, and either commits atomically or is rejected with located diagnostics and repair options, while the model keeps the creative choices and decides how to recover. Reads relate stored analysis of the footage to each use of it on the timeline. In a controlled experiment, a real model is shown 277 of its own committed edits after damaging them. It corrected nearly every call with full or minimal feedback, but locating each problem cut the input tokens a correction needed to less than half, and its corrections dropped other values the model had written in one case rather than seven.

papers.title: A Tutorial on Generative Models for Music Audio
papers.abstract: Music audio generation spans instrumental clips, full songs with vocals, edits of existing recordings, and systems that play alongside a musician in real time. This monograph explains the methods behind these systems for readers familiar with neural-network training who are new to music generation. It introduces neural audio codecs and autoencoders, autoregressive and masked token models, diffusion and flow matching, sampling acceleration, and preference optimization in a shared notation. Worked examples connect training objectives and sampling procedures to published systems. The application sections relate the musical requirements of instrumental generation, songs, editing, and live performance to model design. Comparison tables record representations, methods, inputs, tasks, and release information documented in papers and official sources. Symbolic composition, speech, and sound effects are included where they connect to music audio. We explain how to interpret automatic metrics and learned judges, design and report listening tests, and assess evidence about data provenance, memorization, attribution, and output detection. Selected legal decisions and disputes illustrate the implications for training and release. The reviewed systems combine established generative paradigms with new representations, planning stages, and post-training procedures. Differences in data, scale, and evaluation limit what cross-system comparisons can establish about the sources of reported gains.

papers.title: Influence of Agent Number and Behavior on Users' Psychological Responses in VR Evacuation Training
papers.abstract: This study aims to build effective drill software by combining a virtual simulation of a disaster with multiple agents capable of expressing emotions. We evaluated how the number of agents and their emotional and behavioral actions during evacuation influence users in a virtual space. The results showed that users tended to act more confidently when many agents evacuated with them, and that the evacuation route chosen by the agents influenced the users' decision-making. These findings indicate that users' evacuation behavior is shaped not only by the environment itself but also by the collective behavior of surrounding agents, underscoring the need to consider how agent behavior affects users' psychological states during training.

papers.title: TSM diff: A new Parallel-Tree-Traversal Algorithm for the Comparison of Music Score Files
papers.abstract: Music score files are more difficult to compare than their text-based equivalents, as their content is more complex and organised into hierarchical structures. This explains the lack of tools for processing music scores similar to the widely used old Unix diff command. We propose a new algorithm and tool for comparing digital music scores in various encodings, such as MusicXML or MEI, based on a graph-structured abstract representation called Tree Score Model (TSM). Given two scores, after conversion into TSM, our procedure calculates jointly: A list of differences, localised by time positions in the input scores; A time distance, cumulated duration of time-spans where scores differ; An edit distance, called surface distance, based on notational attributes not related to time. The two later measures are normalised and combined into a similarity distance between scores. Our procedure has been implemented in C++ and is available as a Python module. Our first experiments have shown a very good efficiency even on challenging data. As a proof of concept, we propose two demos based on different versions of some Mozart's piano sonata, and transcriptions of monophonic soli on the same jazz standards by different performers. https://tsm-diff-lbd-7a7e2a.gitlab.io/demo.html

papers.title: Well-Typed ComfyUI Cannot Go Wrong: Gradual Refinement Types for Generative-AI Workflow Graphs
papers.abstract: Generative-AI workflows are programs assembled from independently developed models and operators. Their correctness depends on relationships among model families, tensor geometry, control modalities, and quantization levels. In ComfyUI, these relationships can be violated even when every connection is accepted by its validator, causing expensive runtime crashes or silent failures. To measure how often such semantic composition failures occur, we classify all 8,766 issues and 1,368 discussion threads of ComfyUI's GitHub repository with an LLM, checked for cross-model agreement. They account for 8\% of issue reports and 21\% of issue-tracker runtime failures, and 32\% of them are silent. Because execution cannot reliably reveal those failures, we present ComfyTy, a gradual refinement type system that checks component compatibility before execution as a compositional property of workflow graphs. Each node declares a reusable schema that states which model families, sizes, modalities, and quantizations it accepts and produces. Wiring nodes together combines their schemas into constraints, which ComfyTy solves to find and report incompatibilities. To evaluate ComfyTy, we first inject faults into official ComfyUI workflows and execute every resulting graph. ComfyTy detects 66.4\% of the confirmed injected faults, all of which ComfyUI's own validator admits. On real workflows across more model families, it raises no false alarm on 765 known-good workflows and detects 67\% of 108 failures rebuilt from user reports. Finally, in a user study with 10 participants, its diagnostics raise fault-localization accuracy on faulty workflows from 35.0\% to 87.5\% and repair accuracy from 30.0\% to 62.5\%.

papers.title: SelectSep: Target-Selective Video Queries for Audio Source Separation
papers.abstract: Video-queried sound separation (VQSS) aims to isolate a target sound from an audio mixture using its corresponding video as a query. However, scene-level video queries can become ambiguous when multiple sounding objects are visible, particularly when the target and interferer are semantically similar. We propose SelectSep, a target-selective VQSS framework that jointly uses text and a single click coordinate to specify the target source and instance without requiring segmentation at inference time. We adapt the visual encoder through target-feature distillation with text and click conditioning, and then fine-tune the separator using the adapted visual features. We also introduce an on-screen interference setting, where both the target and interferer are visible, to evaluate target selectivity. Experiments on standard benchmarks and the on-screen interference setting demonstrate consistent improvements in separation quality and target selectivity, particularly for mixtures containing semantically similar sources.

papers.title: Do Open-Source Video Ad Clients Follow VAST 4.3? An Empirical Study of Player Conformance
papers.abstract: Context. Video ads reach streaming and connected-TV apps through VAST documents, and companies count ads from the HTTP requests the player's client library sends. A tracking error can leave playback intact and surface later as disagreeing counts. Objective. To measure how far open-source VAST clients meet the player duties of VAST 4.3, whether verdicts depend on the runtime, what generated inputs add, and when deviations were introduced. Method. A catalog of 108 requirements was extracted from the specification. Six open-source clients in eight configurations ran against 69 crafted test vectors and the IAB's sample tags, under Node.js and in five browsers on three engines, with every request recorded. Grids, fuzzing and a sweep over 36 releases extend the catalog; Google's closed IMA SDK is a comparison. Results. The open-source clients have 78 findings and 3 to 21 must-level deviations per configuration. None of the tested open-source clients that follow redirect (Wrapper) chains fills the required macros in a Wrapper's request; the archived IMA 3.794.0 configuration tested does. One library's timeout throws an exception no caller can catch, ending a Node.js process. In a pod (ads played back to back), one player credits a finishing ad's completion to the next ad, fixed in release 5.3.0. A library can conform under jsdom and deviate in every tested Chrome- and Safari-family browser. Conclusions. The tested clients diverge on the duties other companies use to count and diagnose ads. A shared conformance suite run in real browsers could expose most graded deviations; the harness and vectors are released.

papers.title: Discovering shared interpretable operations in image compression autoencoders
papers.abstract: With the increasing adoption of deep learning for applications such as image compression, improvements in the rate-distortion trade-off have been achieved at the cost of increasingly larger and more opaque ''black-box'' models. Autoencoders are among the most widely used architectures for this task; however, without a clear understanding of their internal behavior, these models tend to grow in complexity to achieve more performance gains. In this paper, we investigate whether universal behaviors can be detected from the internal operations of bias-free autoencoders through Jacobian analysis. If such behaviors exist, they may be extracted to design low-complexity image compression models inspired by high-complexity deep learning architectures.

papers.title: GSVC: Efficient Video Representation and Compression Through 2D Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract: In this work, we explore 2D Gaussian splat as a new primitive for representing and compressing videos, showing its promise as an alternative to traditional signal-based primitives. We introduce GSVC, a new Gaussian splatting-based video codec that incorporates common techniques used in classical video codecs to exploit temporal redundancy between nearby frames. In GSVC, each frame is represented by a set of overlapping Gaussian splats, which, when rendered together, approximate the original frame. Gaussian splats for the first frame and subsequent frames following scene changes (called anchor frames) are learned from scratch, while the remaining frames (called propagation frames) are initialized from the Gaussian splats of their previous frames and then fine-tuned. Scene changes are detected through loss differences during the training process. To capture large motion or newly appeared objects, we randomly add Gaussian splats to propagation frames before fine-tuning. GSVC supports a knob for rate-distortion trade-offs through controlling the number of Gaussian splats for each frame. Gaussian splats with low contributions to the frame quality can be removed during training. GSVC supports two-pass encoding by propagating the Gaussian splats from a future propagation frame back to an anchor frame, further improving the video quality for challenging video scenes. To achieve efficient compression, GSVC uses a residual-based Gaussian splats quantization framework that encodes only changes to the Gaussian parameters between frames. Experimental results show that GSVC achieves rate-distortion performance comparable to state-of-the-art video codec implementations for AV1 and VVC. GSVC inherits the advantages of Gaussian splatting in rendering, allowing it to achieve the rendering speed of 1500 fps for a $1920\times 1080$ video. Project page: https://longanwang-cs.github.io/gsvc/.

papers.title: SemMSA: Latent Semantic-Aided Robust Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Incomplete Data
papers.abstract: Recent research on Multimodal Sentiment Analysis (MSA) has focused on learning from language, visual, and acoustic modalities with incomplete data to infer human sentiment. Most studies typically compensate for missing information by reconstructing modality features or designing complicated fusion mechanisms. However, these methods still suffer from spurious generation and noisy guidance due to the lack of high-level semantic grounding in partially observed multimodal evidence. To address these issues, we propose SemMSA, a latent semantic-aided framework that constructs rich sentiment-relevant semantics with LLMs, fully integrating with all modalities via anchor-free spectral alignment. It mainly consists of Cross-modal Semantic Refinement (CSR) and Cross-modal Spectral Alignment (CSA). Specifically, CSR first adaptively extracts visual and acoustic representations by corresponding adapters to form a unified multimodal prefix with language in the frozen LLM embedding space. It then iteratively produces continuous discriminative semantic states through a token-efficient latent refinement process without decoding explicit text. Next, CSA simultaneously aligns the refined semantics with all modalities by enhancing the dominant spectral component of their kernel Gram matrix. This captures global nonlinear dependencies among all representations without relying on a predefined anchor modality. In addition, an instance-level spectral separation constraint preserves cross-sample discriminability and mitigates representation collapse. Extensive experiments on SIMS, MOSI, and MOSEI benchmarks demonstrate that SemMSA achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers.title: Self-Learning Surprise Detection in Spatial Audio for Viewport-Aware 360-Video Streaming
papers.abstract: Adaptive streaming of 360-degree video relies on viewport prediction to allocate bandwidth efficiently. Current approaches predominantly use visual saliency or historical gaze patterns, neglecting the role of spatial audio in guiding user attention. This paper presents a self-learning framework for detecting "surprising" auditory events, moments that deviate from learned temporal expectations, and demonstrates their utility for viewport prediction. The proposed architecture combines SE(3)-equivariant graph neural networks with recurrent temporal modeling, trained via a dual self-supervised objective. A key feature is the natural modeling of temporal attention decay: surprise is high at event onset but diminishes as the listener adapts. Experiments on the AVTrack360 dataset show that integrating audio surprise with visual cues reduces bitrate waste by up to 18% compared to visual-only methods.

papers.title: Trigger Timing, Deadline Readiness, and Event-Aligned Accounting for Dynamic Ad Insertion
papers.abstract: An ad break in a live stream is a hard deadline. Once a cue arrives, the ad path has seconds to produce a state the player can use, and starting that work earlier buys time while giving the prepared state longer to expire before the break. Comparing trigger policies means scoring which of these happened; the records easiest to collect do not. We separate trigger, reach, readiness, playback, billability and measurement in an observed-event ledger, fix the reference-deadline rule before candidates are assigned, and account for contribution over every planned break-session pair, reached or not. Readiness means the declared state is valid at that deadline. We prove when scoring completion by the deadline instead reverses a policy comparison: for monotone playback with a shared latency law, a fixed state lifetime and common coefficients, the reversal occurs when the earlier policy's extra trigger cost falls between its validity gain and its completion gain. A synthetic study of 45,000 scripted sessions matches this condition on monotone paths, a check of its generator, and, outside its assumptions, finds the same reversal in mixtures with restarts, seeks, late joins and pauses. Playhead summaries misclassify up to 41% of reach indicators yet reverse no comparison in the study: maximum-position errors cancel exactly, and terminal-position errors change only magnitudes. Completion scoring reverses the comparison in three of nine short-lifetime conditions, all at the one latency setting where the proved condition holds. The evidence is synthetic by design; code, seeds and event histories are public.

papers.title: MMFact: Simplifying Multimodal Misinformation Detection with Shared Resources and Tools
papers.abstract: Multimodal misinformation detection methods often rely on different preprocessing pipelines and auxiliary resources, making experimental comparisons difficult to interpret. We present MMFact, a collection of shared resources and tools that simplifies this research workflow. It brings together 47 detector implementations and baselines, three multimodal datasets, and prepared materials ranging from semantic features to OCR, image descriptions, and external evidence. Compatible methods can use the same materials, reducing variation introduced by preprocessing and supporting fairer comparisons. A modular training and evaluation framework preserves method-specific designs while providing common experimental procedures. By treating prepared materials as a shared research resource, MMFact helps researchers focus on developing and evaluating detection methods.
